items.title: New from Chicago: A journey through Rome's history and archaeology as seen in a single city block
items.author: 558757297.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
items.content:
Delve into Rome’s lost history through the stories of a single city block.

Cutting through the heart of Rome is Via delle Botteghe Oscure, a time-worn street named for the mysterious “shops” said to run beneath it. History lies thick here, a museum atop a convent atop ancient ruins; layered in are traces of artisans and poets, pilgrims and saints, a Fascist deportation, a communist coffee bar, a political assassination, and shopkeepers, too. These stories all rest upon a single city block, the same place where, in 13 BCE, the triumphal Roman general Lucius Cornelius Balbus built a monumental theater complex in his own honor.

Elizabeth Rodini’s digs deep into this corner of the city, uncovering a set of surprising, often poignant narratives that range across two thousand years. For as the walls of Balbus’s compound decayed and the neighborhood was rebuilt, this block would come to shelter Romans from all walks of life: the daughters of local prostitutes, an earnest young man in search of a bride, an entrepreneur determined to preserve the city’s colorful dialect, a Jewish family recently liberated from the nearby Ghetto, and a band of idealistic archaeologists unearthing a long-forgotten past, as well as a gifted baker, a medieval donkey, and a Renaissance ghost. Their stories survive in archives and artifacts but also in the enduring power of rumor and legend.

On the Street of the Hidden Shops invites us on a captivating journey to one place across many centuries. Its tight urban focus reveals a Rome most visitors miss, while uncovering some of the many Romes that have been largely lost to history.

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Use positive language
items.author: bounces+38uqqg6p9kfkhr65vo9urh445opwzs7h57lq@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about how to communicate more effectively by using positive language. There are two main reasons you should consider communicating this way: You'll be perceived as more collaborative and easier to work with; when you need to deliver bad news using negative language, you'll get much more attention.

Use positive language whenever possible.

When you set a positive tone for your conversations you will be perceived as more collaborative than combative or resistant, and people will feel better about working with you. And when you use negative words, they will stand out and get maximum attention.

In practice, this means avoiding negative words such as “can’t,” “don’t,” “won’t,” “couldn’t,” and “shouldn’t” and finding alternative ways to convey the same ideas using positive words.

Instead of “We can’t do that”, try “What if we tried this?” Instead of “I don’t think that’s a good idea”, you might say, “Let’s keep iterating to see if we can find an even better approach”. The idea is not to be passive-aggressive or evasive, but to be more thoughtful when dismissing ideas, suggesting alternatives, or even delivering bad news.

This gives more weight to any negative message that you need to deliver because you’re only using negative language when you must communicate that something is dire or needs a high level of attention.

It’s a challenge, but this is a muscle that you can exercise and strengthen over time.

items.title: Royals free agent targets: The position players
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
A little over a week since the start of free agency and there's been little movement. Not surprising, but to me, that first large free agent signing...that’s the official start of the offseason. As noted previously in this space, the specter of the owners locking out the players at the start of December means the next several weeks should see a flurry of activity. Already, agent Scott Boras who represents the consensus top free agent Tarik Skubal, is predicting his lefty will sign sometime this month. If that's happening, the whole market could hit frenzy status in the next couple of weeks.

With that in mind, it’s time to focus on the players currently on the market who could help the Royals when they finally play ball in 2027.

The Royals need to be bold this offseason. I mean . If they deem a player on their current roster is simply “good enough,” then they should probably be looking for an upgrade at that particular position. While left field and center field are obvious positions of need for the Royals, I would proffer second base into that mix. Michael Massey had a fine 2026, producing 2.3 fWAR on the back of stellar defense at the keystone. Offensively, he hit .274/.305/.430 which, with a 100 wRC+, was dead-on league average. But this year’s class at second base is deep. There are possibilities there.

As for center, I am intrigued by the presence of Carson Roccaforte in the Royals prospect pipeline. He won a minor league gold glove and went 30/30 with 35 bombs and 32 bags split between stops in Double-A Northwest Arkansas and Triple-A Omaha. He earned that bump to the Storm Chasers later in the season and ended up with 118 PAs over 28 games. That is to say, with such limited exposure to the top of the minors, he probably needs a bit more seasoning to be ready for the show. A stop-gap option in center should remain on the free agent shopping list, although the pickings at that position are extremely slim. And left field has kind of been a disaster since Alex Gordon went south after 2015. Where have you gone, Andrew Benintendi? Royals nation turns it’s lonely eyes to you.

We know the Royals are set at short, third and catcher. First base could probably use an upgrade if you don’t have strong feelings in favor of Vinnie Pasquantino, but free agency is the worst place to look to upgrade that position. Right field is settled for the moment as well. That leaves second (possibly) along with left and center as areas where the Royals could see improvement.

I’ve compiled some names the Royals should be checking on as the free agent market begins to take shape. The names below are not endorsements. Merely, they are players of interest. As such, I'm ignoring the top end of the position player class. Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki are going to be out of the Royals comfort zone. That's not necessarily a bad thing as I'm not sure either one will live up to a four-year (or more) deal. Same for Brandon Lowe. All three received a qualifying offer as well, which would make them even less attractive to a team like the Royals.

Those players of interest I have identified for the Royals are listed with their three-year averages in batting average, on base percentage and slugging. Also noted are their three-year averages in wRC+ and fWAR, along with walk and strikeout rates. And finally, I've posted their initial Steamer projections for the 2027 season from FanGraphs.

2027 Steamer Projection: .304/.344/.406, 110 wRC+, 2.8 fWAR

Nobody finds fewer barrels, swings a slower bat and has a lower hard-hit rate than Luis Arraez. Yet, it somehow just works. That’s because the contact he does make is square…and there’s a lot of it. Just look at those walk and strikeout rates!

Last year he worked with infield guru Ron Washington in San Francisco. The result: An eye-catching turnaround on Arraez’s defense, one of the biggest year-to-year improvements in Statcast history, going from a -11 Run Value to a +10 RV. That’s insane. Granted, most of his number last year came from first base, but he was there because his defense at second was so abysmal. The last time he played primarily second base prior to 2026 was in 2023 when he also finished with a -11 Run Value. Amazing.

Mix the massively improved defense with the steady offense and Arraez experienced a career year at the perfect time. Teams that believe his defensive improvement is sticky, will inflate the price. Even if the glove regresses, there’s value in a .340 OBP with the occasional double down the line.

He's suited up for five teams over the last four years because his skill set isn't valued the way it was 50 years ago. Last year, he had to settle for a one-year, $12 million deal. He will get more this winter, but I'd be leery of getting too carried away.

2027 Steamer Projection: .234/.317/.408, 101 wRC+, 2.3 fWAR

Before you delete this email, hear me out. Jazz Chisholm Jr. is, at his best, a dynamic player. He went for 30/30 in 2025 and, while none of the five tools scream elite, they’re more than good enough to be an above average player and an upgrade for the Royals at second base.

He did slump in 2026, with his home run total dropping to 19 and his strikeout rate ballooning to almost 30 percent because he chased out of the zone more than he had ever before.

The problem is, Chisholm doesn’t always seem to be at his best. In fact, he seemed to wear out his welcome in New York. The Yankees didn’t extend a qualifying offer, so he doesn’t come with that baggage. That makes Chisholm an ideal candidate for a short-term “prove it” contract. Dangle two years at $40 million with an opt out and the opportunity to pair with Bobby Witt Jr. up the middle. See if that will motivate him. I think it will.

2027 Steamer Projection: .265/.310/.383, 92 wRC+, 1.2 fWAR

We know how much Matt Quatraro and the Royals value defensive versatility. Sometimes, like with Nick Loftin, it works. Other times, like with Jonathan India in left, it absolutely does not. Mauricio Dubón is the top utility player on the market this winter. He logged time last year at second, third, short, left and center. He last played first and right field in 2025.

He’s below-average offensively. Last summer, he posted 619 plate appearances, his career high by about 125. Honestly, if a team signs Dubón, they’re looking for the lower end of playing time. He put up 2.2 fWAR in 133 games for Houston in 2024 while posting an 80 wRC+. Last year was one of the better offensive seasons of his career. He should be available for a one-year deal. Two years at $16 million would be the ceiling.

2027 Steamer Projection: .225/.331/.407, 107 wRC+, 1.9 fWAR

Trent Grisham broke out in a big way in 2025, hitting .235/.348/.464 with a 128 wRC+. Great timing on his part as the Yankees tossed a qualifying option his direction that he immediately gobbled up. The encore wasn’t as fun for either Grisham or the Yankees as the center fielder hit just .211/.308/.395 with a 98 wRC+ as he sold out his contact for power more power. He’s also not a great defender in center, but I imagine a team could grab him and drop him in left.

He seems like a guy without a plan at the plate. His swing rate on pitches in the heart of the zone was 67 percent. He doesn’t chase, which is good, but he’s letting a lot of good pitches go by. Hmmmm, I wonder if the Royals have a new hitting coach who is all about planning out plate appearances. Throw him a one-year deal and see if he clicks with Hunter Mense and the rest of the coaching staff to get his offensive mojo back.

2027 Steamer Projection: .230/.336/.406, 108 wRC+, 1.7 fWAR

If I were writing a scouting report on Ian Happ, it would read “a solid regular.” That may be damning with faint praise, particularly for a corner outfielder, but that’s who Happ is as a player.

A switch-hitter who is better from the left side of the plate, he really struggled when hitting right-handed in 2026, batting .145/.217/.267 against southpaws. Yikes. That may be enough to deter the Royals (and other teams) as they search for a good right-handed bat, but you can’t always get what you want unless you’re willing to pay the premium. Again, the question that I return to over and over again in this exercise is, “would this player be an upgrade at his position if the Royals signed him?” That answer feels obvious.

His defense is like his hitting. Good arm. Decent range. Solid, if unspectacular. That’s all you need in left.

A two-year deal around $34 million doesn’t seem out of order. I would not be willing to go three.

2027 Steamer Projection: .236/.302/.415, 97 wRC+, 1.4 fWAR

Look! These aren't endorsements. Merely options. Luis Robert Jr. can’t stay on the field and when he has been on the field the last couple of seasons, he’s been underwhelming. He went for 38 home runs and 20 steals in 2023 and hasn’t been above-average offensively since, so a signing club is rolling the dice that he can tap back in to whatever made him successful just four years ago. To be fair, a lot of his shortcomings can be chalked up to injury. He spent three months on the IL last summer and was a post-trade deadline waiver claim when the Orioles were willing to gamble that he could catch fire the last couple months of the season. He did not catch fire and he’s on this list because the Orioles declined a $20 million option for 2026.

The tools continue to tantalize, but the reality is far different. Maybe worth a flier if you can get him on a one-year deal where he has something to prove. Or you take that flier and get frustrated and let him go for a c-level prospect at the trading deadline. It's probably the latter.

2027 Steamer Projection: .251/.350/.384, 108 wRC+, 2.0 fWAR

To me, Gleyber Torres represents a gamble in the Jonathan India vein. You can squint and see the upside, but odds are against you. Always limited defensively at second, he’s fluxuated between above-average to just plain average at the plate for his entire career. He’s settled more into the latter over the last three years.

Hampered by an oblique injury this year, Torres saw a big decline in his average exit velocity and hard-hit rate and saw his power numbers tumble.

This is his third dip into the free agent pool in as many seasons. He initially signed a one-year, $15 million deal in a move from the Yankees to the Tigers. Last winter, the Tigers dangled the qualifying offer and he accepted. And now he’s back on the open market, looking at yet another one-year deal. He could be a platoon partner with the left-handed hitting Massey at second with Massey also serving as a late-inning defensive replacement. That could be some maximizing.

2027 Steamer Projection: .221/.293/.406, 92 wRC+, 1.1 fWAR

Could I interest you in a project? After hitting 20 home runs in 71 games in 2025 for the Jays, Daulton Varsho had a brutal 2026 campaign where he hit .243/.307/.375 with a 91 wRC+ with the Blue Jays. Dealt to Houston at the trade deadline, he was even worse offensively for the Astros, hitting a brutal .172/.224/.311 over 161 PAs. Turns out, he was dealing with wrist inflammation for most of the year and had surgery at the end of the season to remove a pair of cysts from said wrist. He should be good to go for 2027, which means he’s a candidate for a short-term deal.

He’s made his living in center field, but his arm has never been a strong point and has only declined since he had shoulder surgery a couple of years ago. He’s lost a step (or two) as well. At this point, he’s better suited to left field.

I’m less than enthusiastic about Varsho as an option in Kansas City. The Royals have taken several fliers on alleged bounce-back candidates over the last couple of years and come up completely empty. Varsho gives off those vibes.

Dangle a year at whatever the market rate is; hope for the best and prepare for the worst.

2027 Steamer Projection: .233/.339/.393, 107 wRC+, 1.4 fWAR

It seems like the Royals have been connected to Taylor Ward for three or four years now. If the Royals were going to get him, it was via a trade. Now, he’s on the open market, available for the price of a contract. And maybe some burnt ends as a little bonus.

Traded to Baltimore last winter, Ward was having another one of his solid offensive seasons, although his power numbers took a nosedive. Yet he transformed into something of an on-base machine. Ok…fine. Shipped to Seattle at the trade deadline he went completely south. Totally gone. Like a 117 wRC+ for the Orioles compared to a 23 wRC+ for the Mariners. Some bad luck in the Pacific Northwest with a .180 BABIP, but his Statcast metrics also took a turn. The power remained AWOL and then so did the on base percentage. If you’re going to revamp your offensive game, you should probably make sure the new one sticks.

Ward is also a guy, like Grisholm, who has adjusted his approach at the plate the last couple of seasons where he's much more reluctant to swing. Sure, it's a good thing he's not lurking around the shadow zone, but he's also letting far to many hittable pitches pass by. Again, with the changes the Royals made to their hitting coaching staff the last two seasons, I wonder if there's something there that can be unlocked.

Maybe those last couple of months will drop his price and the Royals can pick him up on a one-year deal. His 2026 season was so weird, I don’t know if I trust him to fully recover.

items.author: SRS0=4gOt=I5=m.ghost.io=bounce+3cffae.7bdc18-misc=muneer.top@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Hi! It's R. Eric Thomas. From the internet?Hi!

What y'all know about wearing orthopedic shoes at the clurb?!

What y'all know about dropping it low but keeping your arch support high, okay?!

What y'all know about breaking a sweat but not your ankle, huh?!

This all started very innocently. I was out with some folks and it got to be around midnight and but one member of the group is like a divining rod for a good time and she wasn't done.

One minute, I was idling on the sidewalk, casually observing her checking Uber and the next minute I was being extraordinarily renditioned into the back of a black van.

Now, I love all my little British spy shows--Black Doves, Slow Horses, The Night Manager, The Day Manager, The Middle Manager--so I'm prepared for this kind of thing to happen. But when we arrived at the club, a dive-y longstanding Philly dance bar called The Dolphin (also the name of a British spy show), I realized I was in trouble.

I dress fairly cool, but I am under no delusion. I am unc. I'm not pressed about this. I, in fact, have nieces and nephews! But unc does not belong in the clurb!

First of all, I was wearing a trench coat I got in Italy (yes, that could be a brag, but also sometimes the truth sounds impressive. I can't help it! I'm addicted to honesty! Selectively! When it serves me!)

I was also wearing the most god-awful ugly chunky orthotic shoes you've ever seen in your life. But my friend paid my cover at the club (a reverse ransom!), so in I went.

Let me explain the shoes. You see, my feet hurt because I be running around in your mind all day.

I don't really need to go into the physiology of it, but I realized last year that a lot of the body discomfort I was feeling was because all my shoes, except my Birks, are cute but ultimately functionless. I am also cute but ultimately functionless, so who is driving the bus?

I looked into footwear options that weren't going to give "Obama on the campaign trail" or "running the marathon this morning" and I found this company, Vionic, that makes a wide variety of shoes, including the aforementioned absolutely hideous, incredibly comfortable white sneaker.

[I originally put a picture of it here but I had to remove it because, out of context, it will absolutely impact your impression of me as a cool, beautiful person.]

The thing is: a hideous, chunky shoe is exactly what Gen Z and Gen Alpha are wearing nowadays. Everyone's wearing these huge pants and something that looks like home insulation on their feet and either a crop top or a one of those parachutes from a kid's birthday party at a soft surfaces gym. No in-between.

I could the youths into thinking I am by wearing these big ass sneakers. And no one would know that these particular ugly shoes are Pop-Pop 3000s and not whatever it is they're wearing.

Now, I used to go to the Dolphin all the time back in the day, the day being Obama-era America, which, chronologically and emotionally, was 1,000 years ago. When I used to go, my favorite night was a throwback night where they played remixes of Motown songs.

Last night was also a throwback night... to 1999.

Specifically, they were spinning hip hop from 1999 and the early 2000s, aka the exact music I was throwing it down to when I first started going to the clurb.

What's worse, every single person in the packed club except our group when these songs that I knew every word to came out.

But who cares! I'm up in the clurb in my Meemah Supremes and feeling

My goodness gracious, do I love a shenanigan. I wasn't there at the clurb to meet anyone or to do anything but bump it to Eve and Mary J. Blige and Lil Kim and Fat Joe and other people who have since been cancelled. I love to dance and you don't have to be under a particular age to be allowed to do it and with my stealthy, fugly shoes, there were no consequences beyond my pride and, honey, who needs that?

When I went to start this post, I was looking for images to go along with it and I googled "old guy at the club" and this is the first link that popped up.

Obviously, I clicked on it, wondering what these 70- and 80-year-olds had to say for themselves.

Beloved, almost every person they interviewed in this article was my exact current age.

You know what, though, good for them. It's a privilege to get older. It's a privilege to go out and experience life. It's a privilege to hear songs that you actually recognize on the dance floor. (Call me when they start blasting Celine Dion at the clurb, honey. I'll be out breaking it down in my Mall Walker X's)

If it's unc behavior to dance it out, enjoy myself, and then wake up the next morning feeling great, then unc I shall be!

up in the clurb in my Meemah Supremes and feeling ,Eric

items.title: The Sunday Ramble
items.author: bounce+2edd00.7bdc18-5mr68b7cb43ac2h04ai5=kill-the-newsletter.com@m.ghost.io
items.content:
The Royals have made a couple of additions to their non-playing staff. First up: They announced the final coach of their major league hitting lab. It's local guy Hunter Mense, who is officially a hitting coach. He will join a staff that includes Connor Dawson as offensive coordinator and Marcus Thames as a hitting coach.

Mense arrives in Kansas City after major league stops in Toronto and San Francisco. A local guy, he grew up in Liberty and went to school at the University of Missouri. Missouri is also where he began his coaching career. He was an assistant coach from 2011 to 2016 and was their hitting coach in 2015 and 2016.

Mense then moved on to the professional ranks and was the assistant hitting coach for the Jays from 2022 to 2025, a time which culminated in their run to the World Series. Working with Toronto’s hitting coach David Popkins, he was originally tabbed to work on swing mechanics and drill design. The 2025 Blue Jays led the majors in batting average (.265), on base percentage (.333) and contact rate (78.5%). They also posted the lowest strikeout rate in the majors at 17.8 percent.

He was brought to San Francisco for 2026 as part of first-year manager Tony Vitello’s staff. Their connection goes back to Mense’s playing days at Missouri. He didn’t have as much to work with in San Francisco as he did in Toronto. Several key Giants got off to a slow start offensively (gee, that sounds familiar!), and there were fingers pointed in Mense’s direction (again, familiar!). They did turn things around as guys like Rafael Devers, Bryce Eldridge and Drew Gilbert all had productive second halves of the year to varying degrees.

He spoke to David Laurilla at FanGraphs back in 2022 about how he focused on improving decisions at the plate and what that did to a plate appearance.

"You’ve always heard about the professionalism of the at-bats, and that’s what you see here (in Toronto). Guys aren’t anxious to swing at every single pitch, because they know that 1) the stuff up here is really good, and 2) they have confidence to hit in every sort of count, in any situation, so they’re willing to take a pitch if it’s not one that they want to drive. They’re willing to wait, wait, wait, wait until they get the pitch they want. What that filters down to is the swing-decision aspect of hitting.

"Decision-making is so key at this level, in part because, again, the stuff is so good. They can expose you so fast, especially if you’re not a good decision-maker. They will find holes really, really fast, and are going to keep exploiting them. If you keep making bad decisions, they’re going to keep going there and expose you."

I'm going to pause right there and say this feels like a fantastic hire for the organization. How many times did it seem like we were watching a hitter over the last couple of years who was just up there hacking? This isn't about what the broadcast loves to harp on in things like "a 75 percent swing" or giving kudos for going the opposite way to move a runner. It's about having a plan to find that pitch you can do damage on. That may be about going the opposite way, which is fine. But again...it's about having a plan and finding the right pitch.

“The one thing that we have to make sure of as coaches, and as an organization, is that when you’re teaching swing decisions, it’s not about taking the balls. It’s about being aggressive on the pitches you want to hit. I think that’s how good coaches teach it. They give guys the freedom to swing at every single pitch that’s in the zone where they can drive the ball. They’re working in areas where they can hit home runs and produce extra-base hits.

“A good decision is just as much swinging at the pitch that you can drive as it is taking the breaking ball that’s out of the zone. Both weigh heavily, and you could even say that swinging at a pitch that you should drive out of the yard is more important. One will get you deeper in the count and might get you a walk. The other one is going to give you a run if you square it up.”

How about that? Make the right swing decisions and you can find a pitch you can rip. So simple, yet kind of complex. I'm excited to see what Mense can do with the hitters on this club.

As Speier recounts in his story, LeVangie has been a part of just about every aspect of the Red Sox organization during his time with the team. He was an advance scout for the Sox from 2006 to 2012 and was given credit for preparation work that culminated in Boston's 2007 World Series title. He then moved to the major league staff, first as a bullpen coach (2013-2019, picking up another ring in '13) and then as a pitching coach in 2018 and 2019. When the Red Sox won a title in 2018, pitcher Rick Porcello called LeVangie "the heart and soul of our staff."

LeVangie shifted over to the pro scouting staff after the 2019 season.

LeVangie's role with the Red Sox exceeded that of a conventional bullpen coach. Almost any adjustment made by a Boston pitcher in recent years came with some input from LeVangie. He's the one who suggested that Drew Pomeranz switch sides of the rubber — right before Pomeranz submitted the best prolonged stretch of his career. He's the one who was on top of Craig Kimbrel all last season, making sure he kept his mechanics in order. He's the one who back in 2016 helped straighten out Clay Buchholz during his stints in the bullpen.

In fact, if there's one caveat to LeVangie's promotion, one complaint emerging from Boston pitchers, it's this one, from Kimbrel: "I'm going to miss hanging out with him in the bullpen. … He has a game plan every day and understands each guy. As a pitching coach, that’s the number-one thing: understanding everyone has something different and how to work with that."

The story also included praise for LeVangie from guys like Chris Sale and Pedro Martinez. Seems like a couple of good guys to vouch for your pitching bona fides.

No clue what's going on in Boston as they've had something of a brain drain from their front office and field staff over the last couple of seasons. It's wild that someone who has spent over 35 years in an organization in various capacities, how is massively respected, would just pick up and move on. Sure feels like the Red Sox's loss is the Royals gain.

The annual GM meetings open this week in Las Vegas. The buzzword around this yearly confab is “groundwork.” As in, there are never any expectations around this gathering when it comes to moves and signings, but its where the genesis of such deals take shape. There is a slightly different tilt to this year’s edition, given commissioner Rob Manfred and his lockout lust.

Will moves come together quicker than usual? Will this be the week that free agents start to migrate to new clubs? Difficult to tell, but you know what they say about old habits. The current crop of general managers give off a cautious vibe (although there are certainly some exceptions). Given the amount of groundwork (there’s that buzzword!) often necessary to pull off anything these days, I sort of doubt anything seismic develops. The acceleration that everyone is predicting when it comes to the free agent frenzy will come probably in the last week of November.

The Silver Slugger finalists were announced this week. Like with the Gold Gloves earlier, there is a solid Royals contingent among the potential winners.

Bobby Witt Jr. is seeking his third consecutive Silver Slugger at shortstop. I would like to think he’s a shoo-in, but there’s going to be some competition from Detroit’s Kevin McGonigle. McGonigle, who split time between second and short finished ahead of Witt in OBP (.376 to .359), but Witt came out ahead in slugging percentage (.441 to .430). It could swing either way, but I’d bet on McGonigle given he’s pulling up to this honor as the presumptive AL Rookie of the Year. Congrats to the other shortstop finalist Zach Neto of the Angels on his third-place finish.

At catcher, Carter Jensen is a finalist with Detroit’s Dillon Dingler. Feels like there are some good bats up the middle in the AL Central. I make Jensen to be the favorite given he topped Dingler in just about every offensive metric you can pull up. If Jensen does in fact win the award, he will be the sixth rookie catcher to do so. The others? Benito Santiago and Matt Nokes in 1987, Craig Biggio in 1989 and Mike Piazza in 1993. Nice company.

The Royals third finalist is Jac Caglianone. A year ago, did you think we would be talking about Cags being up for any award, let alone this one? While I always believed he would turn things around, I couldn’t say I was expecting anything like what we saw last summer. Caglianone is up against Wilyer Abreu, Randy Arozarena, Cody Bellinger, Cahse DeLauter, Riley Greene, Tristian Peters and Mike Trout. Caglianone’s .494 slugging percentage does top the list of finalists so it’s not like he’s an outsider. I think he has a legit shot.

When you see the Royals having four Gold Glove finalists and three for the Silver Slugger, it only serves to underscore how dreadful the pitching—particularly the bullpen—was this season.

In a blink and you missed it transaction, the Chicago White Sox signed Alec Marsh to a minor league deal. The Royals released Marsh at the end of last month as they were getting their 40-man roster tidied up. He last pitched for the Royals in 2024, having missed time with shoulder soreness that became a shoulder impingement that became labrum surgery.

When the Royals optioned him off the roster, I thought there was a chance he could return on a minor league deal, like the one he signed with the White Sox. Good luck to Marsh going forward. It has to be incredibly frustrating to miss two full seasons due to injury. I hope he can find a way to get back on the field in 2027.

If you have an itch to watch live baseball, you can scratch it with the Arizona Fall League "Fall Stars Game" tonight on MLB Network. The Royals will be well represented with outfielders Angeibel Gomez and Zion Rose and with left-hander Justin Lamkin suiting up to represent the American League.

Gomez, as you know is the second-youngest player in AFL history, has played mostly right field for the Surprise Saguros and hit .306/.390/.444 over 10 games. Just an exciting talent.

Rose has hit .327/.493/.519 with two homers, two triples, 14 walks and 12 steals in 13 games for Surprise.

Lamkin is in Surprise to make up innings he missed after dealing with shoulder issues this year. According to the write-up at MLB.com:

(Lamkin) has been exceptional at getting ahead of hitters early with his fastball while showing two good breakers in his curveball (a relatively new pitch) and slider, leading to a 3.52 ERA and a 0.78 WHIP in four starts (15 1/3 innings).

The game is scheduled to start tonight at 7 CST.

items.title: New from Chicago: A full-color visual history of how we connected the world
items.author: 557489585.1998257.813949133233@e2ma.net
items.content:
A beautifully illustrated, first-of-its-kind chronicle of road maps through the ages.

Road maps are the most common form of map that most of us regularly interact with while we all seek to find our way from here to there. Today, the digital maps on our devices are just the latest in a series of cartographic innovations designed to make transportation of people and goods easier and more predictable. Whether traveling on foot, in a vehicle, or by animal, people have long created and relied on roads, and efforts to map these overland routes predate the invention of the printing press. Yet the vast majority of road maps have been produced only within the last five hundred years—and even more specifically within the last century.

Historian Jeremy Black is the first to chart the tale of road maps, beginning with the “Peutinger Map,” which illustrated the roads famously connecting the Roman Empire. From the time of antiquity, Black guides the reader through the centuries all the way to the modern age, when the invention of the automobile spurred the creation of roads and road maps like nothing before. Over the course of this journey, Black illuminates the integral role maps played in the development of government infrastructures through time and across all the inhabited continents. And, arriving in the present day, Black shows how technology may soon make the paper road map obsolete even as it builds on the conventions of the preceding centuries.

Featuring a series of full-color maps from the British Library’s collection and beyond,

is an eye-opening visual story of how modern civilizations traversed, constructed, and connected their worlds.

items.title: Leadership Dispatch: Bad surprises are bad
items.author: bounces+p9ugg2oe7li9hdkx6n2aqhpp0kw46trhklpz@ckespa.joshdoody.com
items.content:
This week's Leadership Dispatch is about avoiding bad surprises. Good leadership is often about : You have to decide when to share bad news and when to handle it yourself. But you should always strive to avoid sitting on bad news so long that it becomes a bad surprise for your team.

If you see bad news coming, don’t sit on it and hope things change for the better. Make sure you communicate that bad news early so the team can either prevent it or plan for it.

It can be very easy to think you might save the situation before it gets bad, or that maybe things won’t turn out as bad as you expect. Hope is not a strategy. The longer you wait, the worse the surprise.

How much you share will depend on whether you’re sharing up, sharing with co-leaders, or sharing with the team you’re leading. When sharing up and with co-leaders, share more and share faster. When sharing with the team you’re leading, share more selectively, but do not allow your team to be blindsided by bad news.

You should also strive to share bad news along with some sort of plan or at least a suggestion to prevent or mitigate it. It’s much easier to receive bad news if it’s paired with a plan of action.
